5	
6	What explains this degradation? 7

9

11	
12	Our experiments yield five findings: (1)~degradation operates through two channels---count-driven recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp at intermediate schema sizes for document-level RE) and confusability-driven type substitution (typical-batch gap ${\approx}\,2.2$\,pp; quartile $\Delta = -5.3$\,pp)---an asymmetric relationship where count dominates, consistent with bounded interaction in RE (TOST $p = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp) but coupled in NER where NER recall exhibits non-monotonic recovery at full-schema; (2)~pairwise SCS predicts type confusion ($r = 0.112$--$0.129$), the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE; (3)~effects are consistent across schema sizes and granularities (BCS slopes: $p = 0.60$; DocRED: slope $= -0.71$, $R^2 = 0.53$), and directionally consistent across prompt designs, with attenuated magnitude under improved prompts; (4)~per-type aggregation is confounded by centrality on homogeneous schemas; (5)~NER decomposition fails due to merge amplification; RE confusability-aware grouping yields no significant improvement over random (+1.4\,pp, $p \approx 0.19$, n.s.) despite oracle routing recovering +29.8\,pp.
13

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Training-free\footnote{We use ``training-free'' and ``zero-shot'' interchangeably to denote prompting without parameter updates.}\footnote{Code and data will be released upon acceptance. Anonymous review materials: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/schema-dag-extraction}} LLM information extraction---prompting a large language model with a target schema and asking it to extract structured information without any task-specific fine-tuning---enables rapid deployment across new domains and ontologies. This zero-shot paradigm eliminates the need for labeled data, making it attractive for applications where annotation is expensive or schemas evolve frequently \cite{llm4ie-survey-2024}. Yet the paradigm carries a critical limitation: performance degrades sharply as the number of candidate types in the prompt schema grows. On named entity recognition, recall drops from 0.72 with a single candidate type to a plateau of ${\sim}$0.27 across intermediate schema sizes (22--44 types) before partial recovery at full-schema. On relation extraction, accuracy falls from 85.7\% with one relation to 50.4\% with 80 relations (sentence-level) and from 88.0\% to 38.7\% with 96 relations (document-level)---near or exceeding halving. This degradation is not academic: real-world ontologies routinely define 50--200+ types, placing them squarely in the regime where training-free extraction becomes unreliable.

What explains this degradation? Prior decomposition strategies \cite{uniner-2024,llm-pee-2025,parse-2025} conflate two mechanisms: having more types to discriminate among (count) and having semantically similar types to confuse (confusability) (hereafter Channel~1 and Channel~2). None isolates which factor predicts the gains (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).

We ask three questions. \textbf{RQ1}: Does type confusability independently predict extraction degradation beyond the effect of type count? \textbf{RQ2}: Through what mechanisms do count and confusability each degrade performance? \textbf{RQ3}: Can confusability-aware schema decomposition improve extraction quality?

To our knowledge, we present the first controlled study isolating type confusability from type count via stratified design in zero-shot LLM IE, spanning NER, RE, and event detection (ED). We operationalize confusability via the \emph{Schema Confusability Score} (SCS)---pairwise embedding cosine similarity---and its batch-level aggregation, the \emph{Batch Confusability Score} (BCS). We evaluate on Few-NERD \cite{fewnerd-2021}, FewRel \cite{fewrel-2018}, DocRED \cite{docred-2019}, and MAVEN \cite{maven-2020} using Qwen3-32B (\S\ref{sec:experimental_setup}).

Our experiments yield five findings: (1)~degradation operates through two channels---count-driven recall decline (up to $-$49\,pp at intermediate schema sizes for document-level RE) and confusability-driven type substitution (typical-batch gap ${\approx}\,2.2$\,pp; quartile $\Delta = -5.3$\,pp)---an asymmetric relationship where count dominates, consistent with bounded interaction in RE (TOST $p = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp) but coupled in NER where NER recall exhibits non-monotonic recovery at full-schema; (2)~pairwise SCS predicts type confusion ($r = 0.112$--$0.129$), the first factor empirically isolated in controlled zero-shot IE; (3)~effects are consistent across schema sizes and granularities (BCS slopes: $p = 0.60$; DocRED: slope $= -0.71$, $R^2 = 0.53$), and directionally consistent across prompt designs, with attenuated magnitude under improved prompts; (4)~per-type aggregation is confounded by centrality on homogeneous schemas; (5)~NER decomposition fails due to merge amplification; RE confusability-aware grouping yields no significant improvement over random (+1.4\,pp, $p \approx 0.19$, n.s.) despite oracle routing recovering +29.8\,pp.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Count dominates confusability by ${\sim}20\times$ in typical batches.} Through stratified design isolating count from confusability, we show count effects ($-$42\% to $-$56\% recall) dwarf typical confusability effects (2.2\,pp), counter to decomposition literature's implicit assumption that confusability is the primary bottleneck. Interaction is bounded (TOST $p = 0.003$ at $\pm 3$\,pp) in RE but not in NER, where boundary and type ambiguity couple (\S\ref{sec:multi_channel}).
\item \textbf{Pairwise embedding similarity predicts type confusion.} SCS correlates with confusion rates ($r = 0.112$--$0.129$), with centrality confound identified on homogeneous schemas---invalidating naive per-type aggregation (\S\ref{sec:scs-validation}).
\item \textbf{BCS generalizes across tasks.} BCS--accuracy slopes are consistent across schema sizes ($p = 0.60$) and replicate at document level (DocRED: $R^2 = 0.22\text{--}0.53$) (\S\ref{sec:bcs_controlled}).
\item \textbf{Schema decomposition exposes merge limitations.} Naive merge strategies (union, confidence-gated) collapse NER precision from 0.56 to 0.21; confusability-aware RE grouping yields no significant improvement (+1.4\,pp, $p \approx 0.19$, rank 13/15 random seeds) despite oracle ceiling (+29.8\,pp), leaving routing as an open challenge (\S\ref{sec:sdgd}).
\end{enumerate}
